site.title: Top 10 Executive Coaches — GCC
site.tagline: An editorial ranking of executive coaches practising in the Gulf, curated on published evidence.

about.h1: About this ranking: how Gulf coaches are assessed

blocks.meta: This page sets out the rubric applied to every entry on this list of coaches practising in the Gulf. Nothing in it is held back, so a coach on the list or off it can follow the reasoning from start to finish.

blocks.h2: What the GCC list is, and the question it asks

blocks.p: This is an editorial ranking of executive coaches practising in the Gulf. One named individual curates it, and every entry is put together from public information. Placement cannot be bought, inclusion is never charged for, and no coach is asked to approve an entry before it is published.
Fame in the region is not the test. The test is whether a coach has visibly advanced the practice and taught it in the open.

blocks.small: Every score is an editorial judgement against the published record, not the output of a formula. The percentages describe where the emphasis lies; they are not arithmetic from which a rank falls out automatically, and to suggest otherwise would be false precision.

blocks.p: To score teaching in public, three to five recent pieces by each candidate are read against six markers, and the score is based on the best three published in the last 24 months. Each entry cites the pieces read, so that a reader can test the judgement rather than accept it.

A large part of the recognition available to executive coaches flows from one connected network. Thinkers50's Coaching Legends programme is run in partnership with Marshall Goldsmith's 100 Coaches, the Thinkers50 coaching award bears Goldsmith's name, and a large proportion of the coaches it has honoured belong to 100 Coaches.

Counting a Legend induction, a Coaches50 listing, 100 Coaches membership and a Goldsmith endorsement as four independent validations would considerably overstate how independent they are. On this list that network is one signal, counted at the level of its strongest single element. Recognition from genuinely separate sources, for example peer-reviewed publication, a university appointment, governance of a professional body or national press coverage, is counted on its own and given more weight for being independent.
The curator is subject to the same adjustment as every coach on the list.

blocks.h2: Recognition that does not count, and why

blocks.p: Writing on a paid platform is not marked down. The platform simply cannot serve as evidence of recognition. Being published on a fee-paying platform tells a reader nothing about the quality of the thinking, and good work appears on such platforms routinely. The one thing it cannot do is substitute for independent judgement, since no one independent selected the piece.

ul: Councils and expert panels charge for membership. Posts a coach publishes through them are read and scored on merit, the same as any other writing; the membership is never counted as recognition.

Global Gurus gives public website votes 30% of the weight in its own published methodology, is open to self-nomination and is funded by advertising. A position on it is reported as a placement on a partly public-vote listing and is never described as an award.
Paid directory listings, sponsored profiles and awards with entry fees are kept out of the recognition score completely.

blocks.p: Ignored entirely: follower counts; superlatives a coach claims for themselves, unless a named third party can be shown to have said them; client logos where the engagement has not been publicly disclosed; and any claim without a source that can be cited.
Without a definition this criterion would be a matter of taste. These are the observable proxies it is scored on:

ul: Each factual claim can be traced to a public source that can be cited, and the access date is recorded.

Credentials are reported as published, not as verified, unless they have been checked against the issuing body. The ICF register states in its own disclaimer that ICF does not verify the qualifications listed, so entries say “as published by” instead of implying that the register was checked.
If a claim cannot be sourced, it does not appear. No gap is filled by estimate or inference.
Superlatives are credited, where they appear, to the person who made them.
Clients are named only when the client or the coach has disclosed the engagement in public.

blocks.p: Corrections supported by evidence are made when requested, and each one is logged. A listed coach who asks to come off the list is taken off promptly and without argument. The address is {contact}.
Placement on this list is not for sale. Should that ever change, every affected entry would be marked as advertising, and this methodology would be void.

This site is reviewed quarterly. The network's three rankings, this one, the women's list at csuitecoach.org and the global list at cxocoaches.com, are reviewed in staggered months, one each month, so each list keeps a genuine quarterly rhythm and the three do not all change on the same day. Changes from one edition to the next should be small, a position or two and only on evidence. If most of the names moved every quarter, it would not be a ranking.
Every cycle checks each live claim again, renews sources and access dates, assesses the nomination queue against these criteria, and ends with a dated changelog saying what moved and why.

curator.h1: The curator of the GCC list

blocks.meta: A full account of who owns this site, who decides the Gulf ranking, and what the decisions rest on.

blocks.p: This site and its ranking of executive coaches practising in the Gulf are owned, curated and published by {curator}, an academic who also practises as an executive coach. The ranking is his editorial judgement: it applies the published methodology to evidence taken from public sources.

ul: Besides this domain, he owns the two sister rankings in the network: the women's list at csuitecoach.org and the global list at cxocoaches.com.
He has no ranked entry on any of the three. The person deciding the list is not on the list.
Placement is never bought. Coaches are not charged for inclusion and are not contacted for approval ahead of publication.

Because he practises as an executive coach, he is a competitor of several coaches on this list. For that reason the methodology, the weighting and each exclusion are all published in full, so that his reasoning can be checked instead of trusted.
He is subject to the interlink adjustment in the methodology on exactly the same terms as any coach listed.

blocks.h2: An academic's reason for doing this

blocks.p: The profession is under sustained pressure, and largely fair pressure, for its lack of an evidence base. Coaching rankings have tended to carry the same weakness: they recycle self-reported accolades, present paid placements as honours and repeat superlatives that nobody can source.

This ranking is built the other way round. Published and peer-reviewed work carries weight; the writing is read, not counted; recognition that proves to be one network endorsing itself is discounted; and whatever could not be verified is printed as unverified.
Send corrections, removal requests and any editorial correspondence to {contact}.

nominate.h1: Nominate a coach practising in the Gulf

blocks.meta: At every quarterly review, nominations are assessed against the published rubric. You can nominate yourself or another coach. A place is never guaranteed, and payment plays no part at any stage.

blocks.p: The most useful nominations name particular published work, whether a paper, an essay, a talk or a framework the coach has given away, instead of listing accolades. Tell us what the coach wrote and what made it good.

blocks.h2: What we do with a nomination

ul: Each one is read at the next quarterly review and assessed against the published rubric.
Nominations are held for this review cycle and the next, and are then deleted.

The nominee's details are used editorially. A coach nominated by someone else is not put on any mailing list: no one can give marketing permission for another person. If that coach is listed, they get a single editorial email telling them, which carries its own opt-in link in case they want to hear more.
When you submit, a record of the nomination is created in our mailing system so we can reply to you about it. This is editorial correspondence, not marketing.
To withdraw, write to {contact} at any time.
We do not publish nominations. Coaches who make the list appear in the ranking or under Ones to Watch, and those who do not are not named.

editorial_note: This list asks a different question from its global sister ranking. A trade book with international distribution is a weak proxy for effectiveness in the Gulf, where much of the strongest work is done inside national talent programmes, family-business succession and public-sector leadership development. Ranking Gulf practitioners against a global bibliography would produce a list of expatriate authors rather than the best coaches in the region. Publication therefore carries less weight here, and regional contribution carries more.

Every credential below was checked, and most could not be verified the way readers assume. ICF's Credentialed Coach Finder is an application that cannot be queried by URL, and ICF itself states that "the qualifications of coaches listed, and the information provided is not verified by ICF in any way." Where this list says a credential is verified, it means it appears on an ICF-owned property — strong, but not a registry lookup. Exactly one credential in the entire study was confirmed against the issuing body's own record: Carolann Philips's MCC, on Credly.

Two award programmes are excluded outright. Thinkers360 rankings are membership and self-nomination driven, not independent assessments, and are not treated as recognition here regardless of how they are described elsewhere. The same applies to commercial pay-to-attend industry award programmes, which are cited as self-reported where they appear at all.

Nine of the ten below are women. That is what the evidence produced rather than a target. Every candidate whose credentials could be corroborated on an ICF-owned property was female, and each of the three men in the researched pool carried a disqualifying issue under this methodology — one is an in-house corporate coach a reader cannot hire, one holds no coaching credential, and one asserts two different ICF levels and two different doctoral statuses on a single page.

Disclosed gap. Saudi Arabia is under-represented. The ICF Saudi chapter site blocks automated access, so its leadership could not be resolved. That is a limitation of this edition, not a judgement about Saudi practice, and it is the first thing the January review will address.

coaches.name: Jihane Labib
coaches.role: Founder and CEO, CoachingLab Academy; Chair, ICF Professional Coaches Global Board 2026
coaches.bio: Executive and team coach, and founder of CoachingLab Academy, an ICF Level 1 and Level 2 accredited coach-training provider. ICF's own profile records 15+ years in practice, more than 10,000 coaching hours across 20 countries, and twelve prior years as a marketing and communications director in multinationals, with client sectors spanning FMCG, banking, oil and gas, telecommunications and media.
assessment: She holds the strongest institutional position of any coach in this region: Chair of the ICF Professional Coaches Global Board for 2026, published by ICF itself in its own board announcement. Her MCC and ACTC credentials are corroborated on ICF's own person page rather than only in her marketing — which, given how little in this field survives that test, is the single most important thing about this entry.

Running an accredited Level 1 and Level 2 training provider means she is building capacity for other coaches in a region that has very little of it. On the generosity criterion that counts for considerably more than an individual practice.
notes: Described here as UAE and Morocco, per ICF's own listing, not as a Dubai coach. Her offices are in Casablanca and the Sharjah SPC Free Zone.

Several claims on her own site are excluded because no awarding body or year could be verified: a "Best executive coach 2023" title, MENA Coaching Summit recognition, and an Education 2.0 Conference innovation award which, if real, went to the academy rather than to her.
"First Arab elected to the ICF Global Board" and an EMCC Master Practitioner accreditation are self-claimed and unverified. Performance statistics on her book page are unsourced and are not repeated.

coaches.name: Lina El Assaad
coaches.role: Executive and team coach; Chairperson, ICF Governance Committee; past President, ICF UAE
coaches.bio: Executive, leadership and team coach with more than two decades supporting C-suite leaders, senior government officials and members of royal families, with work across Fortune 500 organisations. Past President of ICF UAE, Chairperson of the ICF Governance Committee, an AoEC coach trainer and a Harvard Business Review Council contributor.
assessment: She holds the only ICF global individual award ever made to a GCC-based coach. ICF's own past-winners archive lists "Lina El Assaad, PCC (UAE)" as an Accomplished Coach for 2023 — and a sweep of that archive from 2005 to 2025 turns up no other person based in the Gulf. On independent third-party recognition, which this methodology weights above self-description, nothing else in the region comes close.
Two decades of practice at head-of-state and royal-family level is a tier of work almost no one in this study can evidence, and her governance roles at ICF are elected by peers rather than purchased.
notes: ICF's profile also describes her as the first PCC to receive its Coaching Impact Award. That is ICF referring to the same award family, not a second honour, and it is not double-counted here.
She has no personal website, which is a genuine gap for a public ranking and the main reason she is not ranked first.
Holds PCC rather than MCC; no other credential is stated on ICF's page. No books.

coaches.name: Dr Clare Beckett-McInroy
coaches.role: Founder, BECKETT MCINROY Consultancy; creator of the CoachME model and TAP360
coaches.bio: Founder of BECKETT MCINROY Consultancy and originator of the CoachME coaching model and the TAP360 team profiling tool. She co-founded ICF Bahrain, where she was Vice President, and ICF Doha–Qatar, where she was President, and has contributed subject-matter expertise on team coaching and supervision to ICF headquarters. EdD, University of Bath.
assessment: MCC and ACTC corroborated on ICF's own person page, plus a doctorate from a serious university — an unusual combination in this field, where research training and coaching credentials rarely sit together. Her CoachME model and TAP360 instrument are published tools other practitioners use rather than proprietary language wrapped around standard practice.

CoachME was named ICF Distinguished Coaching Education Provider in 2023, confirmed verbatim on ICF's own past-winners page. She was also the nominating coach behind the Qatar Financial Centre's 2020 ICF Middle East Prism Award, documented in ICF's own published case study. Co-founding two national ICF chapters is infrastructure work that outlasts any individual practice.
notes: The 2023 ICF award is organisational — it went to CoachME and the consultancy, not to her personally. Recorded accordingly.
"EMCC Coach of the Year" appears on her own site with no year attached and could not be verified. It is excluded.

ICF describes her as author of five books, but no publisher or year could be verified for any of them, and an earlier ICF profile said two. No book count is printed. A "Certified Agile Coach" credential names no issuing body. Her company is registered in Manchester, UK, while she practises from Doha.

coaches.name: Carolann Philips
coaches.role: Executive coach and talent-development consultant; President, ICF Oman Chapter 2025–26
coaches.bio: Executive coach, behavioural-skills trainer and talent-development consultant with more than 25 years across the Middle East and Asia, resident in Oman for over 30 years. Vice President of the ICF Oman Chapter from 2023 and President for the 2025–26 term. Her earlier career included learning and development at Bank Muscat.
assessment: Hers is the only credential in this entire study verified against the issuing body's own record. Her MCC appears on Credly, the platform ICF Credentials and Standards itself uses to issue badges — not on an ICF profile page, not in her own marketing, but at source. Everything else in this field rests on weaker evidence, and that distinction is worth more than a shelf of industry awards.

Her credential stack is unusually broad and independently issued — CPTD from the Association for Talent Development, GPHR from the HR Certification Institute, CELTA from Cambridge, SHL assessment certifications. Honestly, What Do I Do? was published by Notion Press in February 2026.
notes: Four awards appear in her materials — from the World HRD Congress (2017) and the Middle East Training & Development Awards (2019). Both are commercial, pay-to-attend industry programmes with limited editorial standing, and they are recorded here as self-reported rather than as independent validation.
ICF Oman's board pages show her as PCC in 2023 and MCC in 2025–26, consistent with an upgrade; any credential reference should be dated.
She holds a dual role — personal practice plus Managing Director of Hallmark Training Institute. Disclosed.

coaches.name: Leila Rezaiguia
coaches.role: Co-Founder and Managing Partner, Kompass Consultancy; Head of the Academy of Executive Coaching, UAE
coaches.bio: Co-Founder and Managing Partner of Kompass Consultancy in Dubai and Head of the Academy of Executive Coaching in the UAE, confirmed on AoEC's own people directory. Executive and systemic team coach, accredited coach supervisor and ICF mentor coach with 23–25 years across public and private sectors, coaching in English, Arabic and French.
assessment: Heading AoEC in the UAE is verifiable on AoEC's own site and is not a badge that can be bought — the distinction that separates real standing from purchased standing runs through this entire ranking, and she is on the right side of it. Kompass has been AoEC's delivery partner across the GCC and Levant since 2018.

Her client evidence is among the most concrete in the region: named testimonials from the CEO of Abu Dhabi Finance and the Chief of Corporate Affairs at the Dubai Future Foundation, plus a five-year partnership with INSEAD's Career Development for Working Professionals. Named senior clients willing to be quoted are rarer and more informative than award counts.
notes: PCC and EMCC EIA are firm-stated and could not be registry-confirmed. "NLP" is listed with no issuing body and is disregarded.
A separate ESIA supervision accreditation appeared in search results but could not be confirmed against EMCC's register, and is not printed.
No book.

coaches.name: Sameera Ali Baba
coaches.role: Owner, Mubadara for Business Consultancy; Director of Learning and Lead CoachME Faculty MENA; past President, ICF Bahrain
coaches.bio: Bahraini entrepreneur who built her career in training, delivering accredited coach education in both Arabic and English and designing programmes matched to clients' cultural context. Past President of ICF Bahrain, board member of the Bahrain Society for Training and Development, and Director of Learning and Lead CoachME Faculty for MENA at Beckett McInroy Consultancy.
assessment: MCC and ACTC corroborated on ICF's own person page, alongside EMCC Senior Practitioner and ESIA supervisor status. Delivering accredited coach training in Arabic is the substantive point: most coach education reaching the Gulf is imported and English-only, and building it in the working language of the region is a contribution the international recognition bodies have no way of seeing.

Her supervision accreditation matters more than it looks. Supervising other coaches is a generosity marker under this methodology — it is unpaid-in-reputation work that raises the standard of everyone else's practice.
notes: Past presidency of ICF Bahrain is a peer-elected role, not an award. No award verified.
"SCRUM MASTER II" and "CMCC" appear in her credential string with no issuing body stated and are disregarded. A training award from HABC is self-stated with no year.
The "40+ workshops per year" figure is self-reported. No books.

coaches.name: Fatima Nakhjavanpur
coaches.role: Founder and Managing Director, Choice HR Consultancy; faculty, Ashridge / Hult International Business School
coaches.bio: Founder and Managing Director of Choice HR Consultancy, coaching in Dubai and the wider region since 2009. She works with business leaders, professionals and government officials, runs a mentoring programme for young women, and practises in English, French and Persian.
assessment: Her MCC is verified on ICF's own events platform, and that same platform publishes her coaching specialties as "Board level, C-Suite" — one of very few ICF-published confirmations of C-suite practice anywhere in this study. For a ranking of executive coaches specifically, an independent statement of the tier someone actually works at is worth more than a list of certifications.

Faculty membership at Ashridge / Hult and front-of-the-room leadership for the Co-Active Training Institute both put her in front of other practitioners rather than only clients. She gave a live master coaching demonstration at the ICF-MCC MENA Coachathon in May 2023, run jointly by eight regional chapters — demonstrating method in public rather than describing it.
notes: Currency flag. Her site's assets and copy run 2017–2024 and the page was last modified in July 2024. This entry should be re-confirmed at the January review, and readers should verify she is taking clients before approaching her.
No books. A Forbes Middle East interview is linked from her media page but the link is old and was not confirmed to resolve.

coaches.name: Fatema Al Tahoo
coaches.role: Executive and agile leadership coach; President, ICF Bahrain Chapter 2026–2027
coaches.bio: Bahraini coach specialising in agile leadership, team development and executive coaching. She offers one-to-one coaching for team and executive leaders, group coaching linking organisational vision to daily operations, and a proprietary Agile Leadership Coaching Cards product. Director of Events on the ICF Bahrain 2024–25 board and President of the chapter for 2026–2027.
assessment: Her PCC is corroborated in two independent ICF-controlled places — the ICF Bahrain member directory and ICF's global events platform — which is a stronger evidentiary position than most entries in this region manage.

She is a GCC national building a practice in Arabic, and her coaching-cards product is a tangible instrument other practitioners can use rather than a service description. Leading a national chapter at this stage of a career is a meaningful commitment of unpaid time to the profession.
notes: Her own site's page title reads "PPC-ICF" — a typo for PCC, but a careless one on a credential.
Her doctoral-researcher status is self-reported through her ICF bio only, with no institution or programme named, and is not printed as a qualification.

A MENA Coaching Summit 2025 speaking slot is indexed but the page returned empty and it is not asserted here. Site content is largely dated 2023. No book, no award verified. Chapter presidency is an elected role, not an honour.

coaches.name: Dr Soha Chahine
coaches.role: Organisational psychologist; Founder, Forward Training & Consulting FZE
coaches.bio: Organisational psychologist and founder of Forward Training & Consulting FZE, advising CEOs, board members and C-suite executives across government, semi-government, multinational and family-held organisations in all six GCC states. Doctorate in Organizational Psychology; MSc in HR Management and Training; Harvard Business School executive programme in Leading Change and Organizational Renewal.
assessment: She has the strongest publication record in this region by some distance, and it is the reason she is ranked despite the flags below. She writes for Harvard Business Review Arabia with her own author page, was featured in Forbes Bahrain in June 2026, has appeared in Economy Middle East, and delivered a TEDx talk. Writing substantively in Arabic for HBR is teaching in public at a level almost nobody else here reaches.
Practising across all six GCC states as an organisational psychologist rather than a certified-programme deliverer gives her a different and useful vantage on regional leadership.
notes: Her headline recognition is excluded. Thinkers360 "Top 25 Global Thought Leaders" and "Top 50 in Coaching" rankings are membership and self-nomination driven and are not independent awards. They are not counted here, and no ranking that counts them is measuring what it claims to.
A "2026 Global Recognition Award" was announced through a paid press-release wire feed rather than editorial coverage, and is excluded.

A "UN Arab Women Ambassador for Human Sustainability" title is self-stated and could not be verified against any UN source. Her ICF PCC is self-claimed and not corroborated on an ICF property. The HBR Arabia and Forbes Bahrain items are the only recognition treated as genuine.

coaches.name: Gaj Ravichandra
coaches.role: Co-Founder and Managing Partner, Kompass Consultancy; registered psychologist
coaches.bio: Co-Founder and Managing Partner of Kompass Consultancy, the AoEC's GCC and Levant delivery partner. A registered psychologist and high-performance coach who has worked with global corporates, government departments, educational institutions and sporting teams. Kompass states more than 15,000 coaching hours delivered internationally.
assessment: He is included on an explicitly different credential path from everyone else on this list, and the reasoning should be stated rather than glossed: he holds no ICF credential at all. What he holds instead is chartered psychology — MAPS with the Australian Psychological Society, MAICD with the Australian Institute of Company Directors — which is a longer and more regulated qualification route than any coaching certification.
He writes the Kompass blog and has kept it active through 2026, which is more sustained public teaching than most of this region's practitioners produce.
notes: No ICF credential on any page checked — notable given his business partner holds PCC, and a real weakness against the credential criterion. He ranks tenth for that reason.
The registering jurisdiction for "Reg Psych" is not stated anywhere and could not be established.
"Recognised High Performance Coach" is site marketing copy, not an award. No books, no award verified.

ones_to_watch.name: Ebru Goksu Yildirim
ones_to_watch.text: ICF PCC, AoEC faculty, CPCC from the Co-Active Training Institute, ORSC and systemic team coaching. Coaching individuals, executives and teams since 2011 after roughly twenty years as a senior marketing-communications professional across MENAT, working bilingually in English and Turkish.
ones_to_watch.note: She appears here rather than in the ten because she has no independent web presence — she is visible only through two firms' pages — and no books, speaking record or awards could be verified. "NLP" is listed with no issuing body.

ones_to_watch.name: Salman Amjad
ones_to_watch.text: Coaching Lead for the Talent Assessment and Coaching unit at Saudi Aramco, Director of Innovation and Development for the ICF Saudi Arabia Chapter, and a member of the MENA Coaching Culture Council. ICF PCC, stated on ICF's own Converge 2023 presenter page.
ones_to_watch.note: He is an in-house corporate coach rather than an independent practice — a reader cannot engage him — which is why he is named here rather than ranked. He is also the strongest Saudi-based file found, and the clearest illustration of the coverage gap this edition discloses.

ones_to_watch.name: Jeanine Bailey and Marie Quigley
ones_to_watch.text: Co-founders of Empower World, an ICF-accredited coach-training and coaching firm operating from Doha since 2012, with named multi-year testimonials from the Head of HR at Vodafone Qatar and a succession-planning manager at Ooredoo Qatar.
ones_to_watch.note: Both are held back for the same reason: their own website states two different ICF credential levels for each of them on different pages — MCC on one, Associate Certified Coach on another. Quigley's credential line also conflates CPCC, a Co-Active training designation, with ICF's PCC credential, which is precisely the confusion this ranking is built to catch.

not_included.name: Dr Iftikhar Nadeem
not_included.text: Excluded on credential integrity, and named here because the reasoning matters more than the omission. A single team page on his own site asserts, simultaneously: a heading reading "MCC"; body text describing his "Professional Certified Coach (PCC) credential from ICF"; body text describing him as a "PhD candidate" at Canterbury Christ Church University; and a caption reading "PhD in Leadership Coaching." Two different ICF levels and two different doctoral statuses, on one page — with the cautious readings in the prose and the promotional ones in the heading and caption. Neither the credential nor the doctorate is verified by any source that is not his own marketing, and a further claim to have chaired ICF's Global Board for Coaching in Organizations could not be verified against ICF. His practice may well be substantial; the documentation is not, and a ranking that discounts unverifiable claims elsewhere cannot make an exception here.

not_included.name: Dr Maryam Mohammed Al Emadi
not_included.text: President of the ICF Doha Chapter, ICF PCC listed on ICF's own events platform, and quoted in the Qatar Tribune in June 2026 on the four-year partnership between Qatar's Ministry of Public Health and the chapter. Excluded on category rather than quality: she is a Senior Consultant Family Physician and Director of Clinical Operations at Primary Health Care Corporation who coaches within Qatar's public-health leadership system. There is no coaching practice a reader could engage. Chapter presidency is an elected volunteer role, not an award.

outstanding: Saudi Arabia coverage — icfsaudichapter.com blocks automated access, so chapter leadership could not be resolved. A manual pass is the first priority for the January review.
Fatima Nakhjavanpur's practice currency — site last modified July 2024; confirm she is taking clients
Jeanine Bailey's and Marie Quigley's actual ICF credential levels, which their own site contradicts
Whether Rania Laing, PCC — ICF Foundation Trustee and former ICF UAE president — is UAE or UK based; ICF's own 2026 release says United Kingdom while other sources place her in the Gulf
Kuwait: no candidate surfaced at the evidence bar used here. Not an absence of practitioners, an absence of published evidence.
